newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China plans to let Taiwan firms list as A shares.
newsitem.headline: China plans to let Taiwan firms list as A shares.

text.p: Beijing plans to treat Taiwan companies investing in China as national firms and let them list in its stock markets as domestic A shares, local newspapers reported on Sunday.
Quoting unnamed Taiwan investors in China, several newspapers said Beijing planned to allow blue-chip Taiwan firms to list as A shares which can directly raise funds in China and be traded in yuan.

So far, only two Taiwan-funded companies have exceptional treatment to list as A shares -- one is fully owned by Taiwan firms, the other a joint venture with Chinese partners, the Commercial Times said.
Currently, Taiwan makers in China can only apply for listing as B shares, which are traded only in foreign currencies by foreigners.

However, the United Daily News quoted a business leader Wu Chang-ming as saying that in a seminar last Tuesday between Taiwan companies and Chinese officials, Chinese officials said unless Beijing revised related laws, it would be impossible for China to allow Taiwan firms to list as A shares in the near term.
Wu is chairman of the Taiwan business association in Beijing, the paper said.

The Commercial Times quoted Taiwan's vice-economics minister Sheu Ke-sheng as saying the economics ministry could not regulate the listing of Taiwan firms as A shares in China. The decision to list should be left to Taiwan firms themselves, the minister was quoted as saying.

Several newspapers quoted unnamed economics ministry officials as saying the reported China moves aimed to attract more Taiwan funds. But Beijing strictly controls foreign exchange and once Taiwan funds enter China, it will be difficult to withdraw the money.
"The (reported) communist China's move seems to benefit Taiwan firms, but in the long run, Taiwan firms should be careful or else they will be trapped," the Commercial Times said.

Taiwan, separated from China at the end of a civil war in 1949, bans direct contact and investment on the mainland. All investments must be approved by the government and routed through Hong Kong or other third places.
With ties strained recently, Taiwan has expressed concern that its economy may become too dependent on China, thus making it politically vulnerable.
In a prepared address to the National Assembly last week, Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui asked Taiwan businesses to comply with the government's policies.

"Before the hostility across the Taiwan strait is removed ... local businesses and industries should realise that the country's survival and development are far more important than business opportunity," Lee said.
Some 30,000 companies from Taiwan, which China regards as a renegade province, have poured more than US$30 billion into the mainland since an unofficial thaw began in the 1980s.
Taiwan recently drafted a set of criteria to govern local investment in China.

Under pressure from the Taiwan government, Formosa Plastics said on May 7 that it would abandon a US$3 billion China power plant project if Taiwan adhered to its plan to ban firms from investing in utilities and public works there.
